papers.title: Internalizing-peptide engineering converts blocking anti-EGFR antibodies into EGFR lysosomal targeting degraders
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.768013 v1

summary.one_liner: Engineering full-length anti-EGFR antibodies (cetuximab and the LEI antibody) with cell-penetrating arginine-rich peptides converts receptor-blocking antibodies into degraders that reduce total EGFR levels in NSCLC models, including 3D spheroids, alone and with EGFR kinase inhibitors.
summary.plain:
Some cancer drugs that target the EGFR protein only block its signal, while the protein stays on the cell surface. This study attaches short peptides that help cells take in molecules to anti-EGFR antibodies, so the antibody pulls the receptor into the cell where it is broken down. In lung cancer cell lines and 3D cell clusters, the engineered antibody lowered EGFR levels and, combined with kinase inhibitor drugs, slowed growth more than the drugs alone in some tests.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Reducing the amount of a receptor rather than only blocking it is a different strategy from standard EGFR inhibitors, and the text reports gains in combination with osimertinib and gefitinib in lab models. The text is limited to in vitro and 3D cell-culture work, so it does not show whether this helps in animals or patients; it may connect to antibody-based protein degradation approaches more broadly.</plain>
<parameter name="background">- EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) is a cell-surface protein that drives growth signals; it is a target in lung cancer.
- Cetuximab and LEI are antibodies that bind EGFR and block its activity.
- Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) such as gefitinib and osimertinib block EGFR's internal signaling switch.
- Cell-penetrating peptides (here polyarginine, R12) are short chains that help molecules enter cells.
- Endocytosis and lysosomes: cells engulf surface proteins and break them down in acidic compartments; bafilomycin A1 blocks this acidification, used here as a control.
- Recombinant fusion protein: an antibody and peptide made together as one engineered molecule.
- 3D spheroids: clusters of cancer cells grown in culture that mimic some features of tumors.
- LDH release is a standard marker of cell membrane damage.

papers.abstract: Conventional antibodies targeting the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) primarily inhibit receptor activation rather than efficiently eliminating the receptor from tumor cells. Here, we investigated whether engineering full-length anti-EGFR antibodies with internalizing peptides could promote receptor degradation, enhance their biological activity and enable the development of recombinant receptor-depleting antibodies. Chemical conjugation of cetuximab (CTX) to the polyarginine peptide R12 enhanced intracellular uptake, reduced surface-accessible EGFR and decreased total receptor abundance in vitro. CTX-R12 conjugate also enhanced inhibition of wound repopulation in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines, an effect reproduced using the R12 variant LINC18, and transferred to the independent blocking anti-EGFR antibody LEI. Incorporation of LINC19, a variant of LINC18, into recombinant full-length antibody fusion proteins preserved their activity. The LEI-LINC19 fusion (LEIP), reduced surface-accessible and total EGFR, with bafilomycin A1 reversing receptor loss and supporting an acidification-dependent endolysosomal component of degradation. Functional studies indicated that the antibody-peptide reduced DNA synthesis rate. Furthermore, siRNA-mediated EGFR depletion increased TKI-associated reductions in cellular biomass in PC9 cells and increased gefitinib responsiveness in H1975 cells. Consistently, combining LEIP with either osimertinib or gefitinib produced greater inhibition of H1975 wound repopulation than the corresponding individual treatments. LDH analysis revealed increased membrane-damage-associated LDH release following LEIP-gefitinib treatment but no additional increase with LEIP-osimertinib relative to osimertinib alone. These effects extended to 3D NSCLC models. CTX-R12 inhibited PC9 3D colony development, whereas LEIP restricted expansion of established PC9 colonies and reduced the projected area of H1975 spheroids. In H1975 spheroids initiated with 1,000 or 5,000 cells per well, LEIP-containing combinations with osimertinib or gefitinib produced greater inhibition of the spheroid size than the corresponding TKI-only treatments. Nuclear Green DCS1 staining revealed no detectable baseline core necrosis in untreated H1975 spheroids, whereas LEIP treatment was associated with DNA-positive material within and surrounding the spheroids. Moreover, LEIP-treated H1975 spheroids exhibited markedly reduced EGFR immunofluorescence compared with control and parental LEI-treated spheroids. Together, these findings demonstrate that internalizing-peptide engineering of blocking anti- EGFR antibodies can generate full-length EGFR-depleting fusion proteins with enhanced biological activity. The recombinant LEIP format and its activity in 3D in vitro NSCLC tumor models support further investigation of fusion antibody-mediated EGFR degradation as a complementary strategy to EGFR kinase inhibition.

papers.title: Dual photoresponsive hydrogel surfaces enabling integrated single-cell analysis of morphology and gene expression
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.767535 v1

summary.one_liner: A dual photoresponsive hydrogel surface that uses light to trap individual cells in a uniform array, track their shape changes over time, and selectively release chosen cells for single-cell gene expression analysis.
summary.plain: Scientists want to watch how individual cells change shape over time and then check which genes those cells are switching on, but it is hard to do both on the same cell. This paper describes a gel-coated surface that holds cells in place using one kind of light, lets researchers film them, and then uses a second kind of light to melt the gel under chosen cells so those cells can be collected. The authors report using this to link cell shape changes to gene activity, including in invasive cancer cells.
summary.why: Connecting what a cell looks like over time with what genes it is using is a long-standing gap in single-cell research, so a workflow that does both on the same selected cells may be useful for studying cell variability. The text is only an abstract, so the strength of the results, the number of cells, and how well the method compares with existing tools cannot be judged from it.
summary.background:
- Single-cell analysis: studying cells one at a time, since cells in the same sample can behave quite differently.
- Gene expression: how actively a cell is turning its genes into products; often measured by sequencing the cell's RNA.
- Hydrogel: a water-swollen, jelly-like polymer network that can be used as a cell-friendly surface or scaffold.
- Photoactivatable / photodegradable: chemical groups that change or break apart when hit with light, letting researchers control the material with a light beam.
- Morphological dynamics: changes in a cell's shape and size over time, usually tracked by microscope imaging.
- Invasive cancer cell behavior: the tendency of cancer cells to move into surrounding tissue, a key feature of metastasis.

papers.abstract: Integrated single-cell analysis linking time-resolved cellular phenotypic dynamics with gene expression is essential for understanding cellular heterogeneity but remains technically challenging. Here, we report a dual photoresponsive hydrogel that combines a photoactivatable cell-trapping material with a photodegradable hydrogel, enabling light-directed single-cell capture, time-resolved imaging, and the on-demand release of selected cells for downstream gene expression analysis. This approach allows cells to be arrayed at a high density with uniform spacing, facilitating high-throughput monitoring of morphological dynamics. Cells exhibiting phenotypes of interest can be precisely retrieved by localized hydrogel degradation induced by secondary light irradiation and subsequently subjected to single-cell gene expression analysis. Using this workflow in combination with high-throughput real-time image processing technology, we directly link dynamic morphological features to gene expression and demonstrated the ability of the workflow to examine transcriptional alterations associated with invasive cancer cell behavior.

papers.title: Mass Transfer Formulations Shape Oxygen Transport and Tissue Oxygenation in Microvascular Networks
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767880 v1

summary.background:
- Microvascular network: the web of very small blood vessels (capillaries and nearby vessels) that delivers oxygen to tissue.
- Hematocrit: the fraction of blood volume made up of red blood cells; low hematocrit means fewer red cells carrying oxygen.
- Partial pressure of oxygen (PO2): a measure of how much oxygen is available, in mmHg; low values indicate hypoxia.
- Mass transfer coefficient: a parameter describing how quickly oxygen passes between compartments (red cells, plasma, tissue).
- Single-flux vs double-flux: whether oxygen exchange goes only through plasma to tissue, or also directly from red cells to tissue.
- Sensitivity analysis: testing how much results change when an input assumption is varied.
summary.one_liner: A computational study comparing how different mass transfer coefficient formulations for oxygen exchange between red blood cells, plasma and tissue, including a direct red-cell-to-tissue flux, change predicted tissue oxygenation in realistic cerebral microvascular networks.
summary.plain: Brain tissue needs a steady supply of oxygen, which travels through tiny blood vessels and leaks out into surrounding tissue. This paper builds a computer model of oxygen moving through a realistic network of these small vessels, checks it against in vivo measurements, and tests how the choice of equations for oxygen exchange changes the answer. The authors found that the exchange assumptions matter most when red blood cells are sparse and in the smallest vessels, where they shift predicted low-oxygen tissue areas and local oxygen levels.
summary.why: Predictions of how much oxygen reaches brain tissue depend on these modelling choices, so the results suggest that model assumptions can change conclusions about hypoxia (too little oxygen). The text does not describe applications beyond model evaluation, so its practical impact is uncertain.

papers.abstract: Continuous oxygen delivery is essential for cerebral tissue function, yet its local supply characteristics remain incompletely understood. Quantifying oxygen transport in microvascular networks (MVNs) requires a physiologically consistent description of oxygen exchange between vascular compartments via mass transfer coefficients (MTCs). We investigate how different MTC formulations influence oxygen availability and hypoxic burden in realistic MVNs, and whether they produce relevant local differences in tissue oxygenation. A multicompartment oxygen transport model describing exchange between red blood cells (RBCs), plasma, and tissue in realistic MVNs was developed and evaluated against in vivo measurements. Three RBC-plasma MTC formulations were compared: constant, hematocrit-dependent, and hematocrit- and saturation-dependent. Additionally, a double-flux formulation incorporating a direct RBC-to-tissue flux was compared with standard single-flux formulations. Global tissue oxygen distributions were comparable across RBC-plasma MTC formulations, but hematocrit- and saturation-dependent MTC formulations predicted larger hypoxic tissue fractions. The largest differences occurred under low hematocrit, with local plasma oxygen partial pressure PO2 differing by {approx}6 mmHg along representative vascular paths. Introducing the direct RBC-tissue exchange reduced tissue PO2 at low hematocrit and enhanced it at high hematocrit, with the largest differences observed in small vessels. Sensitivity analysis revealed that RBC oxygen diffusivity can alter the double-flux effect magnitude. MTC assumptions substantially influence predicted oxygen availability and hypoxic burden, particularly under low-hematocrit conditions and in small vessels, underlining the need for their accurate definition. The proposed model provides a basis for evaluating these effects, improving the interpretation of oxygen transport predictions in realistic MVNs.

papers.title: Affibody-conjugated hyaluronic acid hydrogels within collagen sponges enhance dose-dependent BMP-2-mediated bone formation and repair of critically sized femoral defects
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.767909 v1

summary.background:
- BMP-2 (bone morphogenetic protein-2): a signaling protein that tells cells to form bone.
- Collagen sponge: a clinically used porous scaffold that carries BMP-2 but releases it quickly ("burst release").
- Ectopic bone formation: bone growing where it is not wanted, such as soft tissue.
- Hydrogel: a water-swollen network of polymer chains; crosslinking density controls how tightly the network is linked and how stiff it is.
- Hyaluronic acid: a natural sugar polymer abundant in connective tissue.
- Affibody: a small engineered protein that binds a specific target, here BMP-2.
- Critically sized defect: a bone gap too large to heal on its own, used as a demanding test model.
summary.one_liner: A hydrazone-crosslinked, maleimide-functionalized hyaluronic acid hydrogel carrying BMP-2-binding affibodies, formed inside clinical collagen sponges, is tested for controlled BMP-2 retention and bone regeneration in ectopic and critically sized femoral defect models.
summary.plain: Doctors often use a protein called BMP-2 to help bones heal, but the collagen sponge that carries it tends to release it all at once, which can cause swelling and bone growth in the wrong places. This paper describes a new carrier made by growing a gel of hyaluronic acid (a natural sugar-based material found in the body) inside the collagen sponge, with small protein binders that hold BMP-2 in place. The authors report that the composite handled better in surgery, kept more BMP-2 than the sponge alone, and increased bone formation in animal tests.
summary.why: Controlling how long a bone-healing protein stays where it is put could reduce side effects of current treatments, and the design lets binding density be tuned separately from gel stiffness. The text reports animal results only, so whether this helps patients remains open.

papers.abstract: Bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2) is a potent osteoinductive growth factor; however, its burst release from clinical collagen sponge carriers can cause inflammation and ectopic bone formation. Alternative delivery vehicles slow BMP-2 protein release through increased crosslinking density, which stiffens the polymer network and can restrict cell infiltration required for bone formation. Here, we introduce a BMP-2 delivery system in which a hyaluronic acid (HA) hydrogel containing BMP-2-specific affibodies is formed within clinically used collagen sponges to retain BMP-2 through protein-material affinity interactions rather than physical entrapment. We developed a maleimide functionalized, hydrazone crosslinked HA hydrogel such that affibody conjugation is chemically orthogonal to network formation, allowing affibody density to be varied independently of crosslinking density. Forming this hydrogel within a collagen sponge produced composite scaffolds with improved surgical handling and BMP-2 retention. Moreover, in vitro, composite scaffolds exhibited minimal swelling while retaining more BMP-2 than the collagen sponge alone. In vivo, composite scaffolds conjugated with BMP-2-specific affibodies improved ectopic mineralization in a BMP-2 dose-dependent manner. In a critically sized femoral defect, composite scaffolds with and without affibodies significantly increased bone volume relative to the collagen sponge. Thus, this composite scaffold effectively integrates the clinically used collagen sponge with a tunable HA hydrogel and BMP-2-specific affibodies to improve BMP-2-mediated bone regeneration and expand the use of naturally derived biomaterials for bone healing.

papers.title: Quantification of cannabidiolic acid in Cannabis sativa using a two-component allosteric protein biosensor
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767439 v1

summary.background:
- CBD is a medicinal compound from Cannabis sativa; CBDA is the acid form the plant makes first and that converts to CBD.
- A biosensor is a molecule or system that signals when it binds a target, here via a color change.
- Nanobodies are small antibody fragments that can be engineered to bind specific molecules.
- Beta-lactamase is an enzyme; in this design, two halves of it are brought together by the ligand so that the enzyme works again and produces a color in a simple assay.
- KD (dissociation constant) measures binding strength; lower nanomolar values mean tighter binding.
- LCMS (liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry) is the standard lab method used as the reference here.
- Limit of detection is the smallest amount reliably measured.
summary.one_liner: A two-component, beta-lactamase-based protein biosensor built from engineered nanobodies is reported that detects cannabidiolic acid (CBDA) selectively, with a single mutation shifting specificity away from CBD and read out by a simple colorimetric assay.
summary.plain: Cannabis growers and quality-control labs need to know how much CBDA, the precursor of the medicinal compound CBD, is in a plant, but the usual measurements need lab equipment. This paper describes a protein-based sensor that binds CBDA and produces a color change, and the authors tested it on crude plant extracts. Their results matched the standard lab method (LCMS) in 95.6% of cases.
summary.why: A cheap, field-deployable test for CBDA could help with crop valuation, harvest timing and quality checks. The text reports the validation only on crude extracts from CBDA-producing biomass, so its performance in real field or industrial settings is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD) is an important medicinal cannabinoid which accumulates in the Cannabis sativa plant as the precursor cannabidiolic acid (CBDA). Measurement of CBDA levels is important for crop valuation, harvest optimisation, and quality control. However, its quantification typically requires laboratory-based analytical methods that are not readily deployable at the point of need. Here, we report the development of an engineered protein biosensor for selective CBDA detection based on chemically induced dimerization of engineered nanobody domains. Here a cannabidiol-responsive nanobody pair was incorporated into a two-component beta-lactamase-based biosensor architecture, such that ligand binding ultimately results in reconstitution of beta-lactamase activity quantified in a simple colorimetric assay. The resulting sensor displayed high affinity for CBD (KD = 1.9 +/- 0.2 nM) and CBDA (KD = 32 +/- 4 nM). Structure analysis informed a single substitution mutation of ligand-binding nanobody to shift its selectivity in favour of CBDA. This minimal modification inverted sensor specificity, generating a CBDA-selective biosensor that showed no detectable activation either by CBD or the immediate biosynthetic precursor, cannabigerolic acid (CBGA). The engineered sensor exhibited nanomolar affinity for CBDA (KD = 21 +/- 2.4 nM), an 8.4-fold dynamic range, and a limit of detection of 0.5 nM. Sensor performance was validated using crude extracts from CBDA-producing biomass and achieved 95.6% agreement with LCMS-based quantification.

papers.title: Biochemical selection on conserved glycans yield a cross-species AAV capsid for efficient panretinal intravitreal delivery
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.17.767272 v1

summary.background:
- AAV (adeno-associated virus): a small, non-disease-causing virus widely used as a gene delivery vehicle; its outer shell (capsid) determines which cells it enters.
- Retina: the light-sensing tissue at the back of the eye; photoreceptors are the cells that detect light.
- Intravitreal vs. subretinal injection: injection into the eye's vitreous gel is simpler and reaches more of the retina, but the inner retinal layers block many vectors; subretinal injection is surgically riskier and treats only part of the retina.
- Glycans: chains of sugar molecules on cell surfaces that viruses often use as docking points. Heparan sulfate (HS) and N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) are two such sugars.
- Directed evolution / in vitro selection: generating many capsid variants and picking those that perform best, here guided by receptor binding.
- rd10 mice: a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration. Laser-induced choroidal neovascularization: an experimental model of abnormal blood vessel growth under the retina.
summary.one_liner: A paper describing CReST, a receptor-guided in vitro selection method that yielded the AAV2.IvtB capsid, which transduces retina more efficiently after intravitreal injection across mice and pigs by engaging terminal GlcNAc on photoreceptors while attenuating heparan sulfate binding.
summary.plain: Gene therapy vectors (harmless viral shells used to carry genes) usually have to be injected under the retina, a surgery that reaches only part of it. This paper looks for a version that can be injected into the eye's gel-filled center instead and still reach the light-sensing cells across the whole retina. The authors mapped sugar-based molecules in the retinas of seven mammals and used those shared features to guide a lab selection method, producing a vector that worked better in mice and pigs.
summary.why: The reported gains are measured in mice and pigs and include partial rescue of photoreceptors in a mouse degeneration model and reduced laser-induced blood vessel growth, so they are preliminary and not yet tested in patients. If the approach holds up, it could make retinal gene therapy simpler to deliver, but the text does not show clinical safety or efficacy.

papers.abstract: Inherited retinal diseases are leading candidates for gene therapy, but photoreceptor-directed adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors still require subretinal injection, which treats only part of the retina and carries surgical risk. Intravitreal delivery is simple and panretinal, yet inner-retinal barriers block most capsids, and capsids selected in one species rarely translate. Mapping retinal glycans across seven mammals, we found heparan sulfate (HS) marking the inner limiting membrane and terminal N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) enriched on photoreceptor segments. These invariants defined a two-part design principle, attenuated HS binding with strong terminal GlcNAc engagement, implemented as a sequential in vitro selection, Conserved Receptor-Selection Technology (CReST). Its lead GlcNAc-selected capsid, AAV2.IvtB, increased retinal transgene expression 6.5-fold over AAV2.7m8 in mice and photoreceptor transduction 2.5-fold in pigs, acting through terminal GlcNAc engagement. It partially preserved photoreceptors in rd10 mice and suppressed laser-induced choroidal neovascularization. CReST is a receptor-guided, animal-free route to capsids with a defined, conserved mechanism.

papers.title: VINCIT: A virus-incorporated biomaterial niche enables spatially controlled in vivo CAR T cell engineering
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.767176 v1

summary.background:
- CAR T cells: a patient's own immune T cells fitted with a synthetic receptor that lets them recognize and kill a specific target, here CD19 on B cells.
- Viral vectors: engineered viruses (adeno-associated and lentiviral) used as delivery vehicles to insert genes into cells; "transduction" means successful gene delivery into a cell.
- Hydrogel / nanofiber composite: a water-swollen, gel-like material built from very fine fibers that can be injected and act as a local depot.
- Humanized mouse model: a mouse given human immune cells or tissues so that human-like immune responses can be studied.
- Neutrophils: common white blood cells that help recruit other immune cells; the paper reports depleting them reduced recruitment and T cell programming.
- Preclinical: tested in animals or cells, not yet in human patients.
summary.one_liner: VINCIT is an injectable nanofiber hydrogel that retains viral vectors locally to recruit immune cells and generate CAR T cells in vivo, reporting spatially confined transgene expression, CD19+ B cell depletion, and extended survival in a humanized lymphoma mouse model.
summary.plain: Cell therapies that reprogram a patient's T cells to attack cancer usually require removing cells from the body and engineering them in a lab first. This paper describes a gel that is injected under the skin and holds gene-delivery viruses in one place, so immune cells that pass through can be modified there and then travel back into the bloodstream. In the mouse experiments described, this local approach confined gene expression to the site better than intravenous virus delivery and transduced more T cells than injecting free virus alone.
summary.why: Making CAR T cells inside the body could avoid the costly, slow manufacturing step and reduce off-target gene delivery to other tissues. The text reports a single treatment extending median survival in a mouse lymphoma model from 32 to 110 days, but this is preclinical work in mice, so its relevance to human therapy is not yet established.

papers.abstract: In vivo generation of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells could bypass the complex manufacturing required for conventional cell therapies, but systemic gene delivery remains limited by off target exposure and inefficient access to target immune cells. Here, we develop VINCIT (Virus Incorporated Niche for Cellular ImmunoTherapy), an injectable nanofiber hydrogel composite that establishes a localized immune-engineering niche for CAR T cell generation in vivo. VINCIT spatially retains viral vectors while recruiting endogenous immune cells, enabling local transduction of T cells, after which the engineered T cells enter the circulation. VINCIT spatially confines transgene expression compared with intravenous viral delivery and markedly enhances T cell transduction compared with subcutaneously injected free virus. VINCIT is compatible with both adeno-associated and lentiviral vectors, and CAR T cells generated in vivo exhibit antigen-specific effector responses and mediate CD19+ B cell depletion. In a humanized mouse model of lymphoma, a single VINCIT administration produces sustained tumor control and extends median survival from 32 to 110 days. Mechanistically, efficient CAR T cell generation requires coordinated interactions among multiple immune populations, with neutrophil depletion markedly reducing cellular recruitment and subsequent T cell programming. These findings establish a localized biomaterial niche for spatially controlled in vivo immune cell engineering.

papers.title: ALI MEA60: A porous thin-film microelectrode array for air-liquid interface electrophysiology of 3D excitable tissues
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.16.766976 v1

summary.background:
- Microelectrode array (MEA): a flat dish or chip with many tiny electrodes that record electrical activity from cells sitting on it.
- Spheroid / organoid: a small 3D ball of cells grown in a dish that imitates some features of an organ, such as brain or heart.
- Excitable tissue: tissue, like nerve or heart muscle, that produces electrical spikes.
- Air-liquid interface (ALI) culture: the tissue sits on a porous membrane with its top exposed to air and its base fed by medium, which improves oxygen and nutrient supply.
- Spikes vs. local field potentials: spikes are fast signals from single neurons; local field potentials are slower signals from groups of cells.
- Impedance and noise: how much an electrode resists current and how much random electrical background it adds; lower values mean cleaner recordings.
- Pharmacological wash-in/wash-out: adding a drug to the tissue and then rinsing it away to see the effect.
- Linear mixed-effects model: a statistical method for tracking repeated measurements from the same samples over time.
summary.one_liner: A porous polyimide microelectrode array with 60 thin-film electrodes and a basal perfusion chamber, designed for long-term air-liquid interface recordings from 3D excitable tissues such as neural spheroids, organoids, and brain slices, characterized for impedance, noise, 60-day stability, and pharmacological responses.
summary.plain: Researchers built a small chip that listens to electrical signals from three-dimensional clumps of nerve or heart cells grown in the lab, and keeps them alive by exposing their top surface to air while feeding them from below. They tested it on 41 devices for electrical noise and resistance, and followed neural spheroids for 60 days, with about 85% of the working channels still working at the end. The chip also picked up the expected drug responses in neural and heart tissue and recorded from brain slices and brain organoids.
summary.why: Long-term recording from 3D tissue is hard, so a standardized, commercially compatible platform with a published stability benchmark could help disease modelling and drug screening. The text does not show how it compares with other devices beyond the authors' own characterization, and its value for those uses is still to be tested by others.

papers.abstract: Objective: Conventional microelectrode arrays (MEAs) are suboptimal for long-term electrophysiology of three-dimensional (3D) excitable tissues, as limited oxygenation, nutrient diffusion, and tissue-electrode coupling compromise recording stability. Air-liquid interface (ALI) culture mitigates these constraints, but existing ALI MEA platforms are limited in channel count, flexibility, and compatibility with commercial multichannel acquisition systems. We developed and comprehensively characterized a next-generation ALI MEA for standardized, long-term recordings across multiple 3D excitable tissue models. Approach: The novel ALI MEA60 is composed of a porous polyimide membrane that integrates an array of 60 thin film microelectrodes (59 recording, one reference) and a basal perfusion chamber with Luer-lock connectors for controlled medium exchange and pharmacological wash-in/wash-out. It is compatible with the MEA2100-Mini data acquisition system (Multi Channel Systems). We characterized electrode impedance and noise across 41 ALI MEA60 devices, assessed 60-day stability with human iPSC-derived neural spheroids (N = 7 MEAs, 121 recordings) using a standardized longitudinal framework and linear mixed-effects models, and evaluated its versatility through pharmacological assays and recordings from human neural spheroids, brain organoids, ex vivo brain slices, and cardiac organoids. Main results: The platform showed reproducible electrical performance (median impedance 56 kOhms; at 1 kHz) and low noise (approx. 5uV Root Mean Square (RMS) in saline, 10-20 uV in medium), resolving spikes and local field potentials simultaneously. Recording remained stable for at least 60 days, with a stable noise floor and ~85% persistence of initial functional channels. Neural spheroids reproduced the standard qualitative signatures to gabazine, 4-aminopyridine (4-AP), and 6-Cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione/D-2-amino-5-phosphonovalerate (CNQX/D-AP5), while cardiac organoids showed the expected beta-adrenergic response to isoproterenol. The ALI MEA60 can similarly record signals from human brain slices and organoids without hardware modification. Significance: The ALI MEA60 combines ALI culture, chronic recording stability, standardized pharmacological testing and cross-tissue compatibility in a single ready-to-use platform. It also establishes a reproducible framework for benchmarking long-term electrophysiological performance, thereby supporting disease modelling, drug discovery, organ-on-chip technologies and future chronic 3D electrophysiology systems. Keywords: microelectrode array (MEA); air-liquid interface (ALI); 3D excitable tissues; neural spheroids; cardiac organoids; chronic electrophysiology.

papers.title: Reprogramming a thiosulfate bacterial two-component system into a perchlorate biosensor
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766565 v1

summary.background:
- Two-component system (TCS): a bacterial signalling circuit with a membrane sensor (histidine kinase) that detects a molecule and passes the signal to a response protein that switches genes on or off.
- Whole-cell biosensor: a living bacterium engineered so that a gene output, often light or colour, reports the presence of a target chemical.
- Directed evolution: repeated rounds of random mutation and selection in the lab to find variants with a desired trait.
- Computational protein design: software that proposes specific amino acid changes to a protein, here protCAD, which uses physics-informed reinforcement learning.
- Perchlorate: a persistent oxyanion (a negatively charged oxygen-containing ion) found as a contaminant, related to thiosulfate and similar ions.
- Ligand: the small molecule a sensor binds to.
summary.one_liner: The authors reprogram the membrane-bound sensor kinase of a thiosulfate-responsive bacterial two-component system (ThsSR from Shewanella halifaxensis) to respond to perchlorate, combining directed evolution with the protCAD computational design method, and use the result in a whole-cell biosensor.
summary.plain: Bacteria often sense chemicals using a two-part switch: a sensor protein on the cell membrane and a partner that turns on genes in response. This paper takes a bacterial sensor that normally detects thiosulfate and evolves it to detect perchlorate, a pollutant for which no natural bacterial sensor was known. The researchers combined lab evolution, which selects for better variants, with a computer design method, and then tested the resulting engineered cells on unsterile environmental samples.
summary.why: Engineered bacteria that detect specific pollutants could offer cheap, programmable field monitoring, so the approach matters for environmental sensing. The text reports the method and a proof-of-use test, but does not give detection limits or field performance details here, so the practical reach is not yet clear.

papers.abstract: Engineering bacterial two-component systems (TCSs) to sense new molecules would enable programmable whole-cell biosensors, but retargeting membrane-bound sensor histidine kinases is challenging because ligand recognition and signal transduction are tightly coupled. Here, we reprogram the thiosulfate-responsive TCS from Shewanella halifaxensis (ThsSR) to detect perchlorate, for which no naturally occurring TCS sensor has been reported. Using a dual growth selection, we simultaneously selected for perchlorate-dependent signaling and against native thiosulfate responsiveness. This strategy first converted wild-type ThsS into a perchlorate-responsive generalist and then produced specialized variants with improved sensitivity, greatly reduced thiosulfate response, and discrimination against related oxyanions. We next applied the physicsinformed reinforcement learning design method protCAD to functional intermediates identified by directed evolution. protCAD-selected substitutions further enhanced sensitivity or signaling output in specialized sensors, even in backgrounds that were refractory to additional random mutagenesis and gene shuffling. As a final demonstration, we used the engineered TCS sensor in a whole cell biosensor to detect perchlorate in unsterile environmental samples. Together, these results define a productive division of labor between experiment and computation: directed evolution discovers signaling-competent, specificity-altered sequence space, while computation explores that evolved space more completely to refine performance. This evolution-computational strategy provides a framework for reprogramming TCS biosensors toward non-native analytes.

papers.title: CDK phospho-degron tags for dynamic protein regulation
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766399 v1

summary.background:
- Protein degradation: cells tag unwanted proteins so they are broken down; engineering this changes how long a protein lasts.
- Phosphorylation: adding a phosphate group to a protein, often acting as an on/off switch.
- CDK (cyclin-dependent kinase): an enzyme whose activity rises and falls through the cell cycle, driving division steps.
- Degron: a short sequence that marks a protein for destruction.
- Budding yeast: a single-celled fungus widely used as a model organism in cell biology.
- Transcription factor: a protein that switches genes on or off; its abundance sets how strongly those genes are expressed.
- Synthetic biology: designing biological parts and circuits with predictable behavior.
summary.one_liner: The paper introduces modular, CDK-responsive phospho-degron tags derived from the Far1 regulatory region that give tunable, cell-cycle-dependent control of protein stability in budding yeast, and shows they can be combined with localization modules and tuned by culture density.
summary.plain: Cells control their own division with a chemical "on/off" signal: an enzyme called CDK adds phosphate tags to proteins at specific times. This paper builds short, reusable tags based on a piece of the yeast protein Far1 that cause a protein to be destroyed when that signal is active. The authors report that changing parts of the tag gives different destruction speeds and thresholds, which lets them adjust how much of a regulator protein, and the genes it controls, a cell has.
summary.why: Most synthetic biology tools control gene switching at the DNA level, so a set of parts that controls protein stability after translation, tied to a natural cell-cycle signal, could offer a second, faster layer of control. The text does not show how well these tags would work outside yeast or in more complex systems, so their broader usefulness remains to be tested.

papers.abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity underpins cell cycle progression through dynamic and temporally ordered phosphorylation events. While transcriptional regulation has been extensively exploited in synthetic biology, the rational engineering of post-translational signaling circuits remains underdeveloped. Here, we introduce modular CDK-responsive phospho-degron tags derived from the Far1 regulatory region and demonstrate their ability to confer tunable, cell cycle-dependent control over protein stability in budding yeast. By systematically modifying cyclin docking motifs and Cks1 priming sites, we generate degron variants with distinct degradation kinetics and phosphorylation thresholds. These modules enable predictable modulation of transcription factor abundance and downstream gene expression. We further combine CDK-responsive degrons with phosphorylation-controlled localization modules for multi-layered regulation of sequential nuclear import and degradation. We encode multiple kinase activity thresholds within a single protein, demonstrating how complex phosphorylation logic can be compactly implemented. Finally, we show that degron performance is strongly influenced by culture conditions, particularly cell density and associated changes in CDK activity. Together, our results establish CDK-driven phospho-degrons as versatile building blocks for engineering dynamic protein regulation and provide a foundation for constructing synthetic post-translational signaling circuits.

papers.title: CUSTOM-Muscle: Customisable, Shape-Tuneable, Oriented Modular PDMS Scaffolds for Disease-Relevant 3D Skeletal Muscle Engineering
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.766110 v1

summary.background:
- Skeletal muscle: the voluntary muscle that moves the body; its cells fuse into long fibres.
- 3D tissue engineering: growing cells in a three-dimensional scaffold rather than a flat dish, to better mimic real tissue.
- PDMS: a soft, silicone-like polymer used to make the scaffold's frame and supports.
- CAD, stereolithography (SLA) and fused deposition modelling (FDM): computer design followed by two 3D-printing methods used to make moulds or parts.
- Twitch and tetanic force: the force from a single muscle contraction and from sustained, fused contraction, used to judge muscle function.
- Motor neurons: nerve cells that signal muscles to contract; the junction between them is the neuromuscular contact site.
- Laminopathy: a group of diseases caused by faults in nuclear envelope proteins (lamins), often giving misshapen cell nuclei.
- Open-source: designs and code are freely shared so others can reproduce and modify them.
summary.one_liner: An open-source pipeline (CAD, stereolithography and fused deposition modelling) produces customisable PDMS scaffolds for 3D human skeletal muscle and neuromuscular tissue culture, with twitch/tetanic force readouts, motor neuron co-culture, a laminopathy-like nuclear phenotype, and an integrated mechanical elongation device.
summary.plain: Scientists often grow muscle tissue in a dish to study muscle function and diseases, but these models are hard to shape, lack support structures, and often do not behave like real muscle. This paper describes a small, customisable 3D culture platform that anyone can build from open-source designs, which holds muscle cells in a shape that can be tuned. The authors report that it supports muscle cell development, can be combined with nerve (motor neuron) cells, and shows the abnormally elongated cell nuclei seen in a muscle disease called laminopathy. They also built a device that stretches the tissue mechanically.

papers.abstract: Modelling skeletal muscle in vitro offers a powerful approach for studying muscle physiology and disease. Despite their potential, current models offer limited scope to combine customisable three-dimensional architecture and mechanical support with complementary functional readouts. Many also lack key features of native muscle, including cellular maturation, neuromuscular organisation and a physiological mechanical environment, limiting their ability to recapitulate muscle structure and function. Here, we establish a three-dimensional (3D) miniaturised, customisable and multifunctional platform for human neuromuscular tissue engineering. We developed an entirely open-source pipeline combining computer-aided design (CAD), stereolithography (SLA) and fused deposition modelling (FDM) to generate culture platforms with tuneable 3D geometries and mechanical properties, supporting short- and long-term culture. Across the configurations tested, all platforms supported skeletal muscle differentiation and functional assessment of twitch and tetanic forces. Integration with motor neuron cultures enabled the generation of neuromuscular constructs suitable for live imaging, metabolic analyses and identification of putative neuromuscular contact sites. Furthermore, the platform recapitulated aberrant nuclear elongation associated with muscle laminopathies, enabling quantitative assessment of disease-associated nuclear morphology. Finally, to address the critical role of mechanical stimulation in muscle physiology, we designed and fabricated an integrated platform for controlled mechanical elongation of 3D skeletal muscle constructs. By combining architectural and mechanical customisation with complementary functional readouts, this framework enables experiments tailored to how tissue organisation, intercellular interactions and external mechanical cues shape muscle function and disease. Its open-source foundation provides a route to wider adoption and adaptation across tissue engineering and the biosciences.

papers.title: A Three-Dimensional Bioprinted Skin Melanoma Model for High-Throughput Drug Screening
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.06.764888 v1

summary.background:
- Melanoma: a cancer of the pigment-producing cells in the skin; advanced cases often develop resistance to drugs.
- Preclinical model: a lab system (cells, tissue, or animals) used to test drugs before human trials.
- Tumor microenvironment (TME): the surrounding cells and tissue that support a tumor, such as connective-tissue fibroblasts.
- Bioprinting: building tissue layer by layer with a printer that deposits cells and gel material.
- Air-liquid interface: culturing skin with its top surface exposed to air, which lets the outer layer mature as real skin does.
- High-throughput screening: testing many compounds at once, here in a 96-well plate format.
- Fluorescent proteins: genetic tags that make cells glow red or green under a microscope, so each cell type can be counted separately.
- Counterscreen: a control test that identifies compounds acting nonspecifically, such as general poisons.
summary.one_liner: A 3D bioprinted, full-thickness human skin melanoma model with fluorescently labeled tumor and stromal cells is presented as a 96-well platform for high-throughput drug screening that uses dual readouts to flag melanoma-selective compounds.
summary.plain: Melanoma is a dangerous skin cancer that often stops responding to treatment, and standard lab tests in flat cell cultures may not predict how drugs behave in real tissue. The authors built a printed, layered piece of human-like skin with a tumor region, supporting connective tissue cells, and an outer skin layer, so that it can be tested in many wells at once. Using color-tagged cells and automated microscope imaging, they measured tumor growth and the survival of surrounding cells together, and report finding compounds that reduced melanoma cell viability while sparing the surrounding cells.
summary.why: Drug screens that include the tumor's surrounding tissue, and that check whether a compound hurts healthy cells too, could make early drug discovery more realistic for melanoma. The text describes the approach as a promising workflow, but it does not report how well its hits translate to patients, so the clinical value remains to be shown.

papers.abstract: Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, and despite major advances in immunotherapy and targeted therapies, most patients with advanced disease eventually develop treatment resistance. The lack of physiologically relevant, scalable preclinical models that recapitulate the tumor microenvironment (TME) remains a major barrier to identifying more effective therapies. Here, we present a novel high-throughput screening platform based on a bioprinted, full-thickness human melanoma skin model that combines the biological complexity of native skin with the scalability required for drug discovery. The 3D tissue construct comprises a dermal region containing primary human dermal fibroblasts, melanoma tumor-like cell clusters localized at the dermal-epidermal interface, and an overlying differentiated epidermis composed of primary human keratinocytes cultured at the air-liquid interface, thereby recapitulating key structural and cellular features of the melanoma TME. To enable multiplexed, high-content analysis, melanoma cells and fibroblasts were engineered to express red and green fluorescent proteins, respectively, allowing automated confocal imaging to simultaneously quantify tumor growth and stromal viability. This dual-readout strategy provides an intrinsic counterscreen to distinguish melanoma-selective compounds from nonspecific cytotoxic agents. The assay was implemented in a 96-well bioprinted format compatible with high-throughput screening of compound libraries across multiple concentrations. Using this platform, we identified compounds that selectively reduced melanoma cell viability while sparing surrounding stromal cells, demonstrating the value of incorporating the TME into primary drug screens. By integrating bioprinting, human tissue engineering, and automated high-content imaging into a scalable workflow, this platform provides a robust and clinically relevant approach for melanoma therapeutic discovery and has the potential to improve the translation of preclinical findings into effective treatments for advanced melanoma.
